title: Planetary Geology
intro: Why do the rocky worlds look so different today? Look inside a planet (core, mantle, crust and the rigid lithosphere, and how earthquake waves reveal them), follow the internal heat that powers geology and magnetic fields, and see why size decides how long a world stays active. Then meet the four processes that shape every surface (impact cratering, volcanism, tectonics and erosion), learn to date a surface by its craters, and finish with Earth's unique plate tectonics: moving plates, young seafloor, trenches, rifts, faults and hot spots.

learningObjectives.text: Describe the core, mantle and crust of a terrestrial world and explain how P and S waves from earthquakes reveal Earth's interior, including its liquid outer core.
Define the lithosphere (the cool, rigid crust plus uppermost mantle) and the asthenosphere, and explain why smaller worlds have thicker lithospheres.
Explain differentiation as gravity separating molten material by density, with metal sinking to the core.
Name the three sources of internal heat (accretion, differentiation, radioactive decay) and identify radioactive decay as the main one today.
Distinguish convection, conduction and radiation and say where each one carries heat out of a planet.
Use the surface area-to-volume ratio of a sphere (3/r) to explain why larger planets keep their heat, volcanism, tectonics and atmosphere longer.
State the three requirements for a global magnetic field and predict what happens to the field if a planet's core cools or its rotation is slow.
Identify impact cratering, volcanism, tectonics and erosion, classify landforms by the process that made them, and relate crater size to impactor size and volcano steepness to lava viscosity.
Use crater counts to compare the geological ages of surfaces, and explain how size, distance from the Sun and rotation rate shape a world's geology.

Describe Earth's plate tectonics: plate speeds, young seafloor and old continental crust, subduction at trenches, convergent, divergent and transform boundaries, and hot-spot island chains such as Hawaii.

sections.title: Looking inside a rocky world

img.alt: Mercury, Venus, Earth, the Moon and Mars shown to scale, each with a close-up of its surface: craters, a radar view of a volcano, clouds and land, more craters and dry channels.

steps.title: Same start, different faces
bullets: The five **terrestrial worlds** are Mercury, Venus, Earth, the Moon and Mars. All are rocky and all were pounded by impacts when young, so they probably started out looking alike.

Today they look very different: Mercury and the Moon are crowded with craters, Venus has strange volcanoes, Mars has giant volcanoes, a huge canyon and dry channels, and Earth shows every kind of feature.
Those differences built up over billions of years, and most of the change was driven from **inside** each world.
**Planetary geology** extends the study of Earth's rocks to every solid world, so Earth is the best place to start.

img.alt: Pie chart of the gas the solar system formed from: hydrogen 71%, helium 27%, hydrogen compounds 1.4%, rocks 0.4% and metals 0.2%.

steps.title: Built from rock and metal
bullets: The gas cloud the solar system formed from was about 98% **hydrogen and helium** by mass. Rock and metal together were well under 1%.
The inner planets did not collect that hydrogen and helium, so they are made almost entirely of the rare ingredients: **rock and metal**.
That is why each terrestrial world is a metal centre wrapped in rock.

img.alt: A hand pushing a coiled spring back and forth to make a compression wave, and a hand shaking it up and down to make a sideways wave.

steps.title: Earthquake waves: P and S
bullets: Our deepest drill holes reach less than 1% of the way to Earth's centre, so we learn about the interior from **seismic waves**, the vibrations an earthquake sends through the planet. It is like shaking a wrapped present to guess what is inside.
**P waves** (push-pull) squeeze and stretch the rock in the direction they travel. They pass through solids, liquids and gases, and bend when they cross into a new layer.
**S waves** (shear, side to side) shake the rock across their direction of travel. They move only through **solids**, because a liquid cannot pass on a sideways push.
The speed and path of both waves depend on the density, temperature, pressure and makeup of the rock, and on whether it is solid or liquid.

img.alt: Cutaway Earth showing wave paths from an earthquake to a monitoring station: S waves travel only through the mantle while P waves also pass through the core.

steps.title: What the waves reveal
bullets: Stations on the far side of Earth from an earthquake pick up P waves but no S waves. A liquid layer must be stopping the S waves: Earth's **liquid outer core**.
Combining records from many stations shows a solid **mantle**, a dense **core** with a liquid outer part and a solid inner part, and a thin **crust** on top.
The Moon and Mars got the same treatment from seismometers: some left behind by Apollo astronauts, one carried by the Mars InSight lander.
For other worlds we rely on indirect clues: comparing a world's **average density** with the density of its surface rock, gravity measured by spacecraft, magnetic fields and volcanic rocks.

boxes.text: Why can S waves not cross a liquid? A sideways shake travels only if neighbouring particles are bonded tightly enough to drag each other along. In a liquid the particles flow past one another, so the shear wave dies, while a push-pull wave still gets through.
P = Push (passes through anything). S = Shear or Sideways (solids only). No S waves on the far side of Earth = a liquid layer inside.

When asked how we know what is inside Earth, the answer is seismic data from earthquakes. Drilling, X-ray or gamma-ray imaging and probes dropped into volcanoes are distractors. Ch9.1 pt1 slides 4-5; Cosmic Perspective 9.1 Special Topic.

sections.title: Layers by density and by rock strength

img.alt: A wedge cut from Earth labelled from the surface down: continental and oceanic crust, lithosphere, asthenosphere, mantle to 2900 km, liquid outer core to 5100 km and solid inner core to 6378 km.

steps.title: Core, mantle and crust
bullets: Sorted by density, every terrestrial world has three layers. The **core** at the centre is the densest and is made mostly of **iron and nickel**.
The **mantle** around it is a thick layer of medium-density rock rich in silicon and oxygen, with heavier elements such as magnesium and iron.
The **crust** is a thin outer skin of the least dense rock, such as granite and basalt.
Earth's core has a **solid inner core** inside a **liquid outer core**. The inner core is hotter, but the even greater pressure at its depth keeps it solid.
Earth's radius is about 6378 km. The mantle ends about 2900 km down, and the outer core ends about 5100 km down.

Six labelled photos: quartzite, marble, granite peaks, an iron-nickel meteorite, green peridotite and white limestone terraces.

steps.title: Rocks from each layer
bullets: An **iron-nickel alloy**, like the metal in some meteorites, stands in for the core.
**Peridotite**, a dense green rock rich in magnesium and iron, is typical of the mantle.
Granite, quartzite, marble and limestone are lighter rocks of the **crust**.
Seismic models of density at each depth agree: density jumps sharply at the core and is lowest near the surface.

steps.title: Lithosphere and asthenosphere
bullets: Layers can also be grouped by **rock strength**. Over millions of years solid rock can bend and flow, like putty that snaps when pulled fast but stretches when pulled slowly, and warm rock flows more easily.
The **lithosphere** is the cool, rigid outer layer. It is made of the **crust plus the uppermost part of the mantle**.
The lithosphere "floats" on the **asthenosphere**, a warmer, softer layer of the mantle beneath it.

Earth is not full of molten lava: its mantle and crust are almost entirely **solid**. Only the outer core is fully molten, and lava comes from small pockets of partly melted rock below the lithosphere.

img.alt: Cutaways of Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury and the Moon drawn to scale, showing crust, mantle, metal core and a dashed line for the bottom of the rigid lithosphere.

steps.title: Comparing five interiors
bullets: Drawn to scale, all five worlds have a core, mantle and crust. Smaller worlds have relatively **thicker lithospheres**: in Mars, Mercury and the Moon the rigid layer reaches almost to the core, while Earth's and Venus's are thin.
A **thin lithosphere** cracks easily and lets molten rock through. A **thick lithosphere** is strong and blocks it, so volcanoes and new mountains become unlikely.
Mercury's metal core is surprisingly large and the Moon's is tiny, which hints that giant impacts shaped both worlds.
Gravity can slowly mould rock: any rocky body more than about **500 km** across becomes round, while smaller ones stay potato-shaped.

boxes.text: Why do small worlds have thick lithospheres? Their interiors have lost more heat, and cool rock is rigid. As a world cools, the rigid zone creeps deeper and deeper.
Lithosphere = 'stone sphere' = crust + top of the mantle, rigid. Asthenosphere = the soft layer under it. Core = metal, mantle = dense rock, crust = light rock.

The lithosphere is not the layer between the crust and the mantle, not the soft rock below, and not lava: it is the crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle. Cosmic Perspective 9.1 Common Misconceptions box: our planet is not filled with molten lava.

sections.title: Differentiation and the sources of internal heat

img.alt: Cutaway Earth labelled rocky crust of lower density, mantle of medium density, metal core of highest density, and the rigid lithosphere made of the crust and part of the mantle.

steps.title: Differentiation sorts by density
bullets: When a young world was hot enough inside for rock and metal to **melt**, gravity pulled the denser material down and the lighter material rose.
This sorting by density is **differentiation**: dense **iron and nickel** sank to form the core, and lighter rock floated up to make the mantle and crust.
It works like oil and water in a jar: the denser water sinks and the oil ends up on top.
Because all the terrestrial worlds are layered, all of them must once have been molten inside.

img.alt: A cutaway planet with arrows to an impact on its surface labelled accretion, to sparks in the mantle labelled radioactivity, and to sinking material labelled differentiation.

steps.title: Three sources of internal heat
bullets: Geology runs on **internal heat**, not sunlight. Sunlight warms only the top few metres of the ground.
**Accretion**: planetesimals crashed into the growing planet, and their energy of motion turned into heat on impact.
**Differentiation**: as dense metal sank, friction turned its lost gravitational energy into heat, like a brick very slightly warming a pool as it sinks to the bottom.
**Radioactive decay**: unstable atoms of uranium, potassium and thorium break apart, and the fast particles they shoot out heat the surrounding rock.

steps.title: Which heat source still works today?
bullets: Accretion and differentiation added heat only while the planets were **very young**. Their leftover heat is still slowly leaking out.
**Radioactive decay** never stopped, so it is now the **only major source** of new heat inside the terrestrial worlds (uranium-238 is one example).
Decay was even stronger early on, because more radioactive atoms were still around.
High pressure alone does not keep rock hot. When the radioactive atoms run out, Earth's deep interior will cool even though the pressure stays the same.
Early on, impacts melted the outer layers, which started differentiation, which released more heat; with strong early radioactivity the interiors melted all the way through.

boxes.text: Why can sunlight not power volcanoes? Its energy is absorbed in the top few metres of ground and radiated away again. The heat that melts rock deep down comes from the planet itself.
Heat sources = A-D-R: Accretion, Differentiation, Radioactive decay. Only R still adds much heat today.

Convection, conduction, radiation and eruption are ways heat moves or escapes, not sources of heat. Tidal heating matters for some moons such as Io but not for the terrestrial planets. Ch9.1 pt2 slides 2-3; Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.4.

sections.title: How interiors cool and why size matters

img.alt: Cutaway planet with looping arrows of convection in the mantle under a rigid outer shell and wavy arrows of radiation leaving the surface.

steps.title: Convection, conduction and radiation
bullets: **Convection**: heated material swells and rises, cooler material shrinks and sinks, and the motion carries heat upward, just like soup in a pot on a stove.

In Earth's mantle, mostly **solid rock** convects very slowly, a few centimetres a year, in loops called **convection cells**. A piece of rock takes about 100 million years to rise from the bottom of the mantle to the top.

Convection stops at the base of the rigid **lithosphere**. Through the lithosphere heat moves mainly by **conduction**: fast-jiggling atoms pass energy to slower neighbours by contact, as when you touch a hot pan.
At the surface the heat leaves into space by **radiation**, mostly as infrared light. Volcanic eruptions also carry some heat straight up through the lithosphere.

img.alt: A small cutaway planet with a cold, thick rigid shell beside a large cutaway planet with many glowing convection loops in its mantle.

steps.title: Big worlds stay hot longer
bullets: Inside, a hot potato keeps its heat far longer than a hot pea does. Think of a big planet as a small one wrapped in extra rock, and that extra rock works as **insulation**.
The small **Moon and Mercury** cooled within about a billion years. Their lithospheres thickened, mantle convection stopped, and they are now geologically **"dead"**.
Earth, the largest, is still hot inside: mantle convection continues and the lithosphere stays thin, so the surface keeps changing. Venus, almost the same size, is probably nearly as active.
Mars, in between in size, has cooled a lot but may keep some activity.
From most to least geologically active: **Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury, the Moon**.

steps.title: Surface area-to-volume ratio: a worked example
bullets: The heat a planet stores depends on its **volume**, but heat can escape only through its **surface area**.
For a sphere of radius r, surface area = 4πr² and volume = (4/3)πr³, so **surface area ÷ volume = 3/r**. A bigger r gives a **smaller ratio** and slower cooling.

Worked example: a ball of radius 2 km has surface area 16π km² and volume (32/3)π km³, a ratio of 1.5 per km. A ball of radius 6 km has surface area 144π km² and volume 288π km³, a ratio of 0.5 per km.
Tripling the radius cuts the ratio to one third, so each cubic kilometre of the big ball has a third as much surface to lose heat through: it cools about three times more slowly.
To go from one quantity to the other, find r first, then use volume = surface area ÷ (3/r). The Moon's radius is 1738 km and Earth's is 6378 km, so the Moon's ratio is about 3.7 times Earth's.

boxes.text: Why does a thin lithosphere mean an active planet? A hot interior keeps the rigid layer thin, and a thin lithosphere cracks and lets magma through, giving volcanoes and tectonics. As a world cools, its lithosphere thickens until nothing gets through.
Ratio = 3/r: bigger radius, smaller ratio, slower cooling, longer-lasting geology. Big world = hot potato; small world = pea.

Inside the rigid lithosphere heat travels mainly by conduction, not convection. Being bigger does not make a planet's surface warmer: surface temperature depends mainly on distance from the Sun and the atmosphere. Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.5 and Mathematical Insight 9.1.

sections.title: Why some worlds have magnetic fields

img.alt: Iron filings lining up along curved field lines around a bar magnet, next to a model of Earth's magnetic field lines looping out of the planet.

steps.title: A planet-sized magnet
bullets: Earth's **magnetic field** has much the same shape as the field around a bar magnet, with field lines looping from one pole to the other.
It is what makes a compass needle point north.
But there is no giant bar magnet inside Earth. The field is made by moving electric charges, the way an electromagnet works.

img.alt: A battery wired to a coil wrapped around a metal bar, with magnetic field lines looping around the coil.

steps.title: Moving charges make magnetic fields
bullets: In an **electromagnet**, a battery drives electrons around a coil of wire, and the moving charges create a magnetic field.
The more charges are moving, and the faster they move, the **stronger** the field.
So a planet needs some way to keep large numbers of charges moving inside it, and that is the job of a molten metal core.

img.alt: Earth cut open to show its core, with field lines looping around the planet and labels for moderately rapid rotation and electrically conducting, convecting molten metals.

steps.title: Three requirements
bullets: Earth's liquid outer core is **molten metal** that conducts electricity. Internal heat makes it **convect**, and Earth's **rotation** twists the flow, so charges circulate as in an electromagnet.
A global magnetic field needs all three: an interior layer of **electrically conducting fluid** such as molten metal, **convection** in that layer, and at least **moderately rapid rotation**.
Of the terrestrial worlds, only Earth satisfies all three, which is why its field is the **strongest**.

The **Moon**'s core cooled and stopped convecting long ago, and **Mars** no longer has enough core heat for convection, so neither has a global field today. **Venus**, whose core is probably molten, rotates only once every 243 days and has no field. **Mercury** has a weak field, probably from its huge, partly molten core.

img.alt: Two night-sky photos of auroras: purple light above a line of trees and green curtains of light above a snowy landscape.

steps.title: The magnetosphere and auroras
bullets: Earth's field forms a protective bubble, the **magnetosphere**, that steers the fast charged particles of the **solar wind** around the planet.
Some particles are funnelled toward the poles, where they make the upper air glow as **auroras**.
By stopping the solar wind from stripping away the atmosphere, the field has probably helped Earth stay habitable.

boxes.text: Why would cooling end a magnetic field? If the core freezes or stops convecting, the conducting fluid stops circulating, so nothing is left to generate the field, however fast the planet spins.
Field = Fluid metal + Flowing (convection) + Fast spin. Remove any one and the global field fails.

A molten core alone is not enough (Venus spins too slowly) and fast rotation alone is not enough. A metal core under a rocky mantle can be completely solid, as on the Moon. Ch9.1 pt2 slide 9; Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.6.

steps.title: Four processes shape every surface
bullets: Rocky surfaces are remarkably smooth: Earth's tallest mountains rise only about 10 km, less than 1/600 of its radius, like a grain of sand on a globe.
Almost every surface feature comes from four processes: **impact cratering**, **volcanism**, **tectonics** and **erosion**.
**Impact cratering**: asteroids or comets strike the surface and blast out bowl-shaped craters. **Volcanism**: molten rock erupts from inside onto the surface.
**Tectonics**: stresses from inside stretch, squeeze and break the surface. **Erosion**: wind, water and ice wear features down or build them up.
Impact cratering is the only one with a cause from **outside** the planet.

img.alt: A sequence of drawings from top to bottom: an object striking a surface, a fan of debris spraying out, and a wide bowl-shaped crater left behind.

steps.title: How an impact makes a crater
bullets: An asteroid or comet hits at roughly **10-70 km/s** (40,000-250,000 km/h). The energy vaporizes rock and blasts out a crater, and debris rains down over a wide area.
Craters are almost always **round**, because the blast throws material out in every direction, whatever angle the impactor came in at.

Rule of thumb: a crater is about **10 times as wide** as the object that made it (often wider) and about 10-20% as deep as it is wide. A 1 km asteroid digs a crater about 10 km across and 1-2 km deep.
Most craters formed during the **heavy bombardment**, when the planets were young. Small craters far outnumber large ones, because small leftover objects were far more common.

img.alt: An aerial photo of Meteor Crater in the Arizona desert beside an orbital view of Tycho crater on the Moon with its central peak.

steps.title: Two real craters
bullets: **Meteor Crater** in Arizona is more than 1 km across and almost 200 m deep. A metal asteroid only about 50 m wide made it about 50,000 years ago.
**Tycho** on the Moon shows the classic shape: a raised rim and a **central peak**.
The impactor's **kinetic energy**, set by its mass and above all its speed, decides how big the crater is.

img.alt: Three Mars craters side by side: a typical bowl-shaped crater, a crater with mud-like flows from an impact on icy ground, and a smoothed, eroded crater.

steps.title: Crater shapes tell a story
bullets: A large crater can have a **central peak**: for an instant the ground is hot and soft, and the centre rebounds upward, like water splashing back when a pebble drops in, then freezes in place.
On Mars, a simple **bowl** with a sharp rim and a ring of debris is a typical fresh crater.
A crater with a big central bump and flows that look like hardened mud suggests an impact into **icy or wet ground**.
A crater with a worn-down rim and a flat floor suggests **erosion** by ancient rain, so crater shapes reveal past conditions.

boxes.text: Why is a crater so much wider than the impactor? At tens of kilometres per second, the impactor carries huge energy for its size. It explodes on contact and digs out far more rock than its own volume.
Crater ≈ 10 × the impactor. A 1 km rock makes a crater about 10 km wide.

Do not pick 'the same size' or '10-20 percent larger': 10-20% is how deep a crater is compared with its own width. Ch9.2 slide 3 adds that craters are often wider than 10 times; Cosmic Perspective 9.2.

steps.title: Why molten rock rises
bullets: **Volcanism** happens when underground molten rock, **magma**, finds a path up through the lithosphere. Once it reaches the surface it is called **lava**.

Magma rises because it is **less dense** than the solid rock around it, because the surrounding rock **squeezes** it, and because gas trapped in it **expands** as it rises, which can make eruptions violent.
It often collects in a **magma chamber** before erupting.
Volcanoes are described as active, dormant or extinct. Earth may have hundreds of thousands of volcanoes, but only several hundred (about 0.1%) are active.

img.alt: Three views with cutaway blocks: flat lava plains on the Moon from runny lava, the broad shield volcano Olympus Mons on Mars, and steep Mount Hood on Earth from the thickest lava.

steps.title: Thick or runny lava sets the shape
bullets: A volcano's steepness depends on how easily its lava flows, its **viscosity**: water has a low viscosity, honey a high one.
The **runniest lava** flows far before hardening and makes flat **volcanic plains**, such as the dark maria of the Moon.
**Slightly thicker lava** builds broad, gently sloping **shield volcanoes**, such as the mountains of Hawaii and Olympus Mons on Mars. They can be very tall but are not steep.
The **thickest lava** cannot flow far, so it piles up into steep **stratovolcanoes** such as Mount Hood and Mount Fuji. Pressure builds up inside them, so they tend to erupt explosively.

steps.title: Volcanoes on Earth
bullets: Augustine in Alaska is a steep, cone-shaped stratovolcano; Skjaldbreiður in Iceland is a low, broad shield volcano.
Plains and shield volcanoes of runny, dense **basalt** are found on every terrestrial world. Steep stratovolcanoes, made of lower-density, thicker lava, are common on Earth but rare elsewhere.
A volcano's age, how long it erupted and how much lava it produced do not set its slope; the lava's viscosity does.

steps.title: Outgassing builds atmospheres
bullets: Water and gases brought in by planetesimals were trapped inside the young planets, like the gas in a sealed bottle of fizzy drink.
Eruptions and quieter volcanic vents let these gases out. This is **outgassing**; on Earth the gas is mostly water vapour and carbon dioxide.
Nearly all of the atmospheric gas on Venus, Earth and Mars came from planetary interiors this way, and so did the water that rained down to fill Earth's oceans.

boxes.text: Why does thick lava make a steep volcano? Sticky lava cools and stops close to the vent, so each eruption stacks on top of the last. Runny lava races away before it hardens and spreads out thin.
Runny → flat plains. Medium → shield (broad). Sticky → strato (steep). Steepness follows viscosity.

If asked what sets a volcano's steepness, the answer is how easily the lava flows (viscosity), not the eruption's duration, the volcano's age or the volume of lava. Ch9.2 slides 9 and 24. Ch9.2 slide 10 says the gas is mostly CO2; water vapour is also a major part (Cosmic Perspective 9.2).

steps.title: Stresses from mantle convection
bullets: **Tectonics** is the building or reshaping of surface features by forces that stretch, squeeze, bend or crack the **lithosphere**. The word comes from the Greek for 'builder'.
Most tectonics comes directly or indirectly from **mantle convection**. Where convection cells push the crust together it is **compressed** into **mountain ranges**, such as the Appalachians.
Where convection cells pull the crust apart it **stretches** and cracks, opening **rifts and valleys**, such as the Ceraunius Valleys on Mars.
The weight of a volcano can also bend the lithosphere, and a rising plume of hot rock can push up a bulge.
Tectonics and volcanism usually go together, because both need **internal heat**.

steps.title: Tectonics on other worlds
bullets: **Akna Montes** on Venus is a mountain range made by squeezing of the crust; an impact crater sits in the middle of the view.
**Valles Marineris** on Mars is a vast canyon system, roughly 8-9 times longer than the Grand Canyon, opened largely by tectonic cracking.
Some tectonics has happened on every terrestrial world, but Earth has the most.

steps.title: Plate tectonics is special
bullets: On Earth, mantle convection has broken the lithosphere into more than a dozen **plates** that move over, under and around one another: **plate tectonics**.
**Tectonics** is the general process; **plate tectonics** is one particular kind, and as far as we know only Earth has it.
When a question says the surface was disrupted by forces from inside, think tectonics; when it names wind, water or ice, think erosion.

boxes.text: Why does tectonics need a hot interior? The stresses come from mantle convection, which runs only while the interior is hot. On a cooled world with a thick lithosphere, nothing pushes or pulls the surface any more.
Pushed together → mountains. Pulled apart → rifts and valleys. Both are tectonics.
A rift valley is tectonic even if a river later flows along it: the crust was pulled apart first. Cosmic Perspective 9.6 notes that the Rio Grande river came after its valley formed.

steps.title: Erosion by water
bullets: **Erosion** is the breaking down or carrying away of surface rock by **water, ice and wind**, the weather of a planet.
The Colorado River has been cutting the **Grand Canyon** for millions of years; tiny changes each year add up.
The rock layers the river cuts through were themselves built by erosion: sediment piled up on old sea floors and hardened into **sedimentary rock**.

img.alt: Yosemite Valley seen from above, a wide forested valley between steep granite walls and the dome of Half Dome.

steps.title: Erosion by ice
bullets: Slow-moving **glaciers** of the ice ages scraped out **Yosemite Valley** in California, leaving a wide U-shaped valley with sheer cliffs.
Glaciers carve **fjords**, the deep, steep-sided valleys flooded by the sea on coasts such as Norway's, in the same way.
Glacial erosion needs snow and ice that build up and flow, so it depends on a world having water and the right temperatures.

img.alt: Rows of tall orange sand dunes stretching to the horizon in a desert.

steps.title: Erosion by wind
bullets: **Wind** sandblasts rock and wears it away, then piles the loose grains into **sand dunes**.
So erosion can **build up** features as well as wear them down.
Wind is driven by a planet's weather, and faster rotation means stronger winds, so wind erosion depends on how fast a world spins.

img.alt: Aerial view of a river spreading into many channels and sandbars where it enters a lake, with forested land behind.

steps.title: Erosion builds new land
bullets: Rivers carry sediment worn from the land and drop it where they slow down at a lake or the sea, building a **river delta**.
Erosion makes canyons, glacial valleys, fjords, dunes, deltas and lakes. Rift valleys, volcanoes and craters come from the other processes.
The Rocky Mountains were once about twice as tall as today; erosion has worn them down.
Erosion depends on an **atmosphere** and weather, so no other terrestrial world feels its effects as strongly as Earth does.

boxes.text: Why do airless worlds keep crisp craters? With no wind, rain or ice, nothing wears the rims down, so a crater on the Moon can look fresh for billions of years.
Erosion = Water, Wind, Ice. If wind, water or ice shaped it, it is erosion; if the crust itself moved, it is tectonics.

Which feature is not erosion? Sand dunes (wind), canyons (rivers), fjords (glaciers) and deltas (river sediment) all are erosion; a rift valley is tectonic. Ch9.2 slides 16-20; Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.14.

sections.title: Craters as a clock for surface age

img.alt: The Moon photographed from space, with bright areas packed with overlapping craters and a few darker, smoother patches with fewer craters.

steps.title: More craters means an older surface
bullets: Impacts land at random everywhere, and the impact rate dropped sharply when the heavy bombardment ended almost **4 billion years ago**.
So a surface crowded with craters has stayed almost unchanged for billions of years: it is geologically **old**.
A surface with **few craters** must have had its old craters erased by lava flows, tectonics or erosion: it is geologically **young**.
**Geological age** means the age of the surface as it looks today, not the age of the planet. Mercury and Venus formed at about the same time, but Venus's surface is far younger.

steps.title: The Moon sets the clock
bullets: In the bright **lunar highlands** craters overlap craters. Rocks brought back by the Apollo astronauts from there are about **4.4 billion years** old.
The dark **lunar maria** are giant impact basins that were later flooded by runny lava. They have only about 3% as many craters, and their rocks are **3.0-3.9 billion years** old.

Dating Moon rocks tells us how the impact rate changed over time. Because impacts are random, the same rate applies to every terrestrial world, so counting craters on orbital photos gives a surface's age with an uncertainty of a few hundred million years.
Earth's and Venus's active geology has erased nearly all their ancient craters, Mars has kept more, and Mercury and the Moon keep most of theirs.

boxes.text: Why does a smooth patch mean young? Craters only accumulate over time, so a region can have fewer of them only if something wiped the slate clean more recently, usually lava flooding it.
Craters are a clock: many craters = old surface, few craters = young (resurfaced) surface.

A lightly cratered region is younger, not older. It is not explained by 'little volcanism' (volcanism erases craters) or by only one side of a planet being hit. Ch9.2 slide 6; Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.15.

sections.title: Size, distance from the Sun and rotation

steps.title: Size
bullets: **Size** is the most important property. A larger world stays hot inside, so **volcanism and tectonics** keep going and erase old craters.

A larger world also has more **erosion**: more outgassing supplies an atmosphere and stronger **gravity holds on to it**. Small worlds have little outgassing and weak gravity, so they lose their air and have almost no erosion.
A large world's core may stay molten and make a **magnetic field**, if it rotates fast enough.

img.alt: Three planets at increasing distance from the Sun: a hot dry one close in, a blue Earth-like one at an intermediate distance, and a frosty one far away.

steps.title: Distance from the Sun
bullets: Worlds **close to the Sun** are too hot for rain, snow or ice, and hot gas escapes more easily, so there is little erosion.
Worlds **far from the Sun** are too cold for rain or oceans; water and other gases freeze out as ice, so erosion is limited.
At Earth's in-between distance, water vapour can condense into **liquid water**, the strongest eroder. This is sometimes called a 'Goldilocks' position: not too hot, not too cold.

img.alt: Two planets compared: a slowly rotating one with few clouds and a rapidly rotating one with swirling storm clouds.

steps.title: Rotation rate
bullets: Rotation is the main driver of **wind and weather**. Faster rotation means stronger winds and storms, so more erosion.
Slow rotation means less weather and less erosion, even with a thick atmosphere. Venus turns once in 243 days, has little wind at the ground and almost no erosion.
Rotation also matters for magnetic fields: a slow spinner has a weak field or none, even with a molten core.

boxes.text: Why does Earth have so much erosion? It is big enough to have outgassed and kept an atmosphere, at the right distance for liquid water, and it spins fast enough for strong weather. All three properties line up.
Size → internal heat (volcanism, tectonics) and an atmosphere (erosion). Distance → liquid water or not. Rotation → weather and magnetic field.

Larger size means longer activity, heat and atmosphere kept longer, and more erosion, but not a warmer surface: surface temperature depends mostly on distance from the Sun and the atmosphere. Earth and Venus are almost the same size with very different surface temperatures. Ch9.2 slides 21-23; Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.16.

steps.title: A broken lithosphere
bullets: Earth is the only planet shaped mainly by ongoing **plate tectonics**. Its lithosphere is broken into about **16 major plates**, plus many smaller ones, that ride on the softer mantle.
Plates move on average **a few centimetres per year**, about as fast as fingernails grow. They do not sit still between earthquakes.
That adds up: at 2 cm per year, a plate travels 2000 km in 100 million years.
Plate motion is tied to **mantle convection**, powered by Earth's internal heat, and GPS stations now measure it directly.

steps.title: Continental drift
bullets: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed **continental drift**, partly because South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces.
The fit is even better along the edges of the **continental shelves**, the true underwater edges of the continents, and matching rocks and fossils are found on both sides of the Atlantic.
Most geologists rejected the idea for decades, because no force strong enough to move continents was known. The mechanism came in the 1950s and 1960s with the discovery of seafloor spreading.

steps.title: Continents on the move
bullets: About **200 million years ago** all of today's continents were joined in one supercontinent, **Pangaea**.
They have drifted apart at a few centimetres per year, opening the Atlantic Ocean, and they will keep moving; the figure even shows a possible map 150 million years from now.
Plate tectonics, not impacts, volcanism or erosion, has set the **arrangement of the continents**.
Geologists now speak of plate tectonics rather than drift: continents ride along on plates instead of ploughing through solid rock.

boxes.text: Why was continental drift rejected at first? A good idea needs a mechanism. Wegener had strong evidence that continents had moved but no force able to move them; seafloor spreading and mantle convection supplied it later.
Plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow: a few centimetres per year.

Do not choose 'a few kilometres per hour' (far too fast), 'a few millimetres or centimetres per century' (far too slow) or 'only during earthquakes'. An earthquake can jump several metres in seconds, but the long-term average is a few cm per year. Ch9.6 slides 4 and 12. The slides say about 16 major plates; Cosmic Perspective says more than a dozen.

steps.title: New crust at mid-ocean ridges
bullets: At **mid-ocean ridges**, mantle material rises and erupts through the lithosphere, making new seafloor and pushing the older seafloor aside: **seafloor spreading**.
On the age map the youngest rock (red) runs along the ridges, and the rock gets older (blue) farther away on both sides.
Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, one of the few places where a ridge rises above sea level.
Ridges add about 2 km² of new crust a year, enough to replace the whole seafloor in about **200 million years**.

steps.title: Two kinds of crust
bullets: **Seafloor crust** is thin (5-10 km), dense basalt and young: most is a few tens of millions of years old, and almost none is older than about 200 million years.
**Continental crust** is thick (20-70 km), made of lower-density rock such as granite, and old: some of its rocks are nearly **4 billion years** old.
The seafloor also has far fewer large impact craters than the continents, another sign that it is younger.
No other planet shows two such different kinds of crust.

img.alt: Cross-section of the upper mantle under the Pacific and Atlantic with convection cells, new seafloor forming at the mid-Atlantic ridge and seafloor crust sinking at an ocean trench under North America.

steps.title: Subduction recycles the seafloor
bullets: Where dense seafloor crust meets lighter continental crust, the seafloor plate dives under it and sinks back into the mantle: **subduction**. A subduction zone is one kind of **convergent** boundary.
The sinking plate drags the surface down into a deep **ocean trench**; some trenches are more than 8 km deep.
The sinking crust heats up and partly melts. The lightest melt rises into volcanoes along the edge of the continent, adding new **continental crust**; that is why steep volcanoes line many coasts.

Ridges and trenches together work like a **conveyor belt**: seafloor is made at ridges, carried across the ocean, and destroyed at trenches. Continental crust is too light to sink, so it survives for billions of years.

boxes.text: Why is the seafloor young? It is constantly being made at ridges and destroyed at trenches, so no piece lasts more than about 200 million years. Continents ride too high to be pulled under, so their ancient rock remains.
Ridge = make (divergent). Trench = take (subduction, convergent). Seafloor crust: thin, dense, young. Continental crust: thick, light, old.

The seafloor is young because dense seafloor crust is pushed under continental crust and recycled, not because ocean water erodes it or because it is 'closer to the mantle'. Ch9.6 slide 13 says rifts and trenches form at divergent boundaries, but Cosmic Perspective 9.6 places trenches at subduction zones, which are convergent.

steps.title: Convergent: plates push together
bullets: At **convergent boundaries** plates push together.
When a seafloor plate meets a continent, the seafloor subducts, making a trench, volcanoes and earthquakes, as along the Andes.
When two **continental** plates meet, neither is dense enough to sink, so the crust crumples upward into mountains.

The **Himalayas** began rising when the Indian plate ran into the Eurasian plate about 50 million years ago, and they are still getting higher. The Appalachians formed in older collisions and have since been worn down by erosion.

img.alt: View from orbit of the Red Sea between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, with arrows showing the two sides moving apart.

steps.title: Divergent: plates pull apart
bullets: At **divergent boundaries** crust is pulled apart or new crust forms. Mid-ocean ridges are divergent boundaries on the sea floor.
When a **continent** is pulled apart, the crust thins and drops into a long **rift valley**. The **East African Rift**, or Great Rift Valley, is slowly tearing Africa apart.
If rifting continues, the valley floods and becomes a new sea with seafloor spreading. That is how the **Red Sea** opened between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula.

steps.title: Transform: plates grind past
bullets: At **transform boundaries**, also called strike-slip faults, plates move **sideways** past each other.
The **San Andreas Fault** in California marks where the Pacific plate moves northwest past the North American plate. In about 20 million years Los Angeles will lie beside San Francisco.
The rough edges catch, stress builds up, and then they slip suddenly in an **earthquake**, moving several metres in seconds. Earthquakes can happen at any type of plate boundary.

img.alt: Map of the Hawaiian island chain on the Pacific plate with photos of eroded Midway, heavily eroded Kauai, fresh lava on Hawaii, and a sonar image of the underwater volcano Loihi.

steps.title: Hot spots: volcanoes inside a plate
bullets: A **hot spot** is a plume of hot mantle rock rising under a plate, away from any boundary.
The **Hawaiian Islands** formed as the Pacific plate moved northwest over a hot spot that stays put: each island was built over the plume and then carried away.

The Big Island is the youngest, with fresh lava. Older islands such as Kauai (about 5 million years) are deeply eroded, and Midway (about 27 million years) is worn almost down to sea level. A new island, Loihi, is growing under water.
Hot spots can lie under continents too: one heats the geysers and hot springs of **Yellowstone**.

boxes.text: Why do the Hawaiian islands get older toward the northwest? The plume stays in place while the plate moves over it like paper moved over a candle, so each new volcano forms at the southeast end and older ones are carried off and worn down.
Converge = crunch (mountains, trenches). Diverge = divide (ridges, rifts). Transform = sideways (faults, earthquakes). Hot spot = island chain.

Hawaii is not on a plate boundary, so a fault, a collision or a rift is not the answer: a mantle plume (hot spot) inside the Pacific plate built it. The Great Rift Valley is continental crust pulled apart at a divergent boundary. Ch9.6 slides 9 and 11; Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.49.

cards.back: The study of the surfaces and interiors of solid worlds: Earth's geology extended to other planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
Vibrations from an earthquake that travel through a planet and along its surface. Their speeds and paths depend on the density and state (solid or liquid) of the rock, so they map the interior.
cards.short: Earthquake vibrations that map the inside

cards.back: The central, densest layer of a terrestrial world, made mostly of iron and nickel. Earth's has a solid inner core and a liquid outer core.
The thick layer of medium-density rock between the core and the crust, rich in silicon, oxygen, magnesium and iron. Almost entirely solid, but it flows very slowly.
The thin outer skin of a terrestrial world, made of its lowest-density rock, such as granite and basalt.
cards.short: Thin outer skin of light rock

cards.back: A dense, green rock rich in magnesium and iron that is typical of Earth's mantle.
A world's total mass divided by its total volume. If it is much higher than the density of the surface rock, the interior must hold denser material such as a metal core.
cards.short: Mass ÷ volume; hints at a metal core

cards.back: The separation of materials by density inside a molten world: gravity sinks dense metal to the core while lighter rock rises to form the mantle and crust.
Ongoing change of a world's surface by volcanism, tectonics, earthquakes and erosion. Most of it is powered by internal heat.
The heat inside a planet that drives volcanism and tectonics. It comes from accretion, differentiation and radioactive decay, not from sunlight.
cards.short: Heat from within that powers geology

cards.back: Heat deposited when planetesimals crashed into a forming planet: their energy of motion became heat on impact. It was added only when the planet was young.
Heat released as dense material sank toward the core: friction turned the lost gravitational energy into heat. Important early, minor today.
cards.short: Heat from metal sinking to the core

cards.back: Heat from the decay of radioactive atoms such as uranium, potassium and thorium in a planet's rock. It is the only major source of new internal heat today.
The slow rising of hot mantle rock and sinking of cooler rock, a few centimetres a year, that carries heat upward and drives tectonics.
cards.short: Slow overturning of solid mantle rock

cards.back: The transfer of heat from hotter to cooler material by direct contact, as fast-moving atoms bump slower ones. It carries heat through the rigid lithosphere.
Loss of heat by giving off light. A planet radiates its heat into space from its surface, mostly as infrared light.
cards.short: Heat leaving the surface as light

cards.back: Surface area divided by volume. For a sphere it equals 3/r, so a larger world has a smaller ratio, loses heat more slowly and stays geologically active longer.
cards.short: 3/r for a sphere; smaller means slower cooling
cards.src: Ch9.1 pt2 slide 6; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 9.1

cards.back: Describes a world whose interior has cooled so much that volcanism and tectonics have stopped, such as the Moon and Mercury.
A planet-wide magnetic field made by charges moving in an interior layer of conducting fluid. It needs molten conducting material, convection in it, and at least moderately rapid rotation.
cards.short: Needs molten metal, convection, fast spin

cards.back: The region around a planet controlled by its magnetic field. Earth's deflects the charged particles of the solar wind and protects the atmosphere.
cards.short: Magnetic bubble that shields a planet

cards.back: Glowing light in the upper atmosphere near the poles, made when charged particles from the Sun are guided in by the magnetic field and strike the air.
cards.short: Polar sky glow from solar particles

cards.back: The making of round, bowl-shaped craters by asteroids or comets striking a surface. The only one of the four geological processes with an outside cause.
A mound in the middle of a large crater, made when the briefly hot, soft ground rebounds upward after the impact and then hardens.
cards.short: Rebound bump in a big crater

cards.back: An underground pocket where molten rock collects before it erupts through the lithosphere as lava.
Molten rock (lava) erupting from inside a planet out onto its surface. It needs internal heat.
cards.short: Molten rock erupting onto the surface

cards.back: Wide, flat areas made by very runny lava that spread far before hardening, such as the lunar maria.
cards.short: Flat land from very runny lava

cards.back: The release of gases trapped inside a planet through volcanic eruptions and vents. Nearly all of the atmospheric gas on Venus, Earth and Mars, and the water in Earth's oceans, came from it.
The disruption and reshaping of a planet's lithosphere by internal stresses, mostly from mantle convection: compression makes mountains, stretching makes rifts and valleys.
cards.short: Surface reshaped by stresses from inside

cards.back: The wearing down or building up of surface features by wind, water and ice. It makes canyons, glacial valleys, dunes and deltas, and needs an atmosphere.
cards.short: Shaping by wind, water and ice

cards.back: Estimating a surface's geological age from how many craters it has: more craters mean an older surface, fewer mean a younger, resurfaced one.
The age of a surface as it looks today, not of the planet itself. A young surface has been reshaped recently; an old one has barely changed in billions of years.
cards.short: How long since a surface was reshaped

cards.back: Dark, smooth plains on the Moon: huge impact basins flooded by runny lava 3 to 4 billion years ago. They have few craters.
The bright, heavily cratered, oldest parts of the Moon's surface, about 4.4 billion years old.

The theory that Earth's lithosphere is broken into plates that move a few centimetres a year over the mantle, explaining continental motion, seafloor spreading and the two kinds of crust. Unique to Earth among known planets.
Wegener's 1912 idea that the continents slowly move across Earth's surface, inspired by the jigsaw fit of South America and Africa. Now explained by plate tectonics.
The making of new seafloor crust where mantle material rises at a mid-ocean ridge, pushing the older seafloor apart on both sides.
cards.short: New seafloor pushing the old apart

cards.back: An undersea mountain chain at a divergent boundary where mantle material rises and erupts to form new seafloor crust.
Thin (5-10 km), dense basalt crust under the oceans. It is young, usually under 200 million years old, because it is recycled by subduction.
Thick (20-70 km), lower-density crust, mostly granite-like rock, that is too light to subduct, so some of it is nearly 4 billion years old.
A deep trough in the sea floor where a seafloor plate is sinking under another plate at a subduction zone, returning old crust to the mantle.
A place where plates push together. Seafloor meeting a continent gives subduction and a trench; two continents meeting build mountains such as the Himalayas.
A place where plates pull apart and new crust forms, such as a mid-ocean ridge or a continental rift like the East African Rift or the Red Sea.
A long valley that forms where continental crust is pulled apart and thins at a divergent boundary, such as the Great Rift Valley in East Africa. Tectonic, not erosional.
