cards.back: The transform boundary in California where the Pacific plate moves northwest past the North American plate, causing frequent earthquakes.
Set by temperature and rock strength: cool rigid rock above, warmer softer rock that flows slowly below. Both are solid.
Differentiation (dense metal sinking, light rock rising) finished early in a planet's history; mantle convection still goes on today.
cards.short: Done long ago vs still happening

cards.front: Why Mercury's magnetic field is weak
cards.back: Its very slow rotation (a day lasting months): a strong field needs a convecting metal core plus fairly rapid rotation.

quiz.q: Which observation shows that part of Earth's core is liquid?
options: P waves reach the side of Earth opposite an earthquake, but S waves do not
S waves reach the opposite side of Earth, but P waves do not
Drill cores have brought up liquid iron from deep inside Earth
Volcanoes sometimes erupt molten metal from the core
Both kinds of wave speed up as they enter the core
quiz.why: S waves cannot travel through a liquid, so when they fail to reach the far side while P waves still arrive, a liquid layer must be blocking them: the outer core. Drills reach under 1% of the way down, volcanoes erupt rock from just below the lithosphere, not core metal, and the reverse pattern would mean the opposite of what is seen.
quiz.source: Ch9.1 pt1 slides 4-5; Cosmic Perspective 9.1 Special Topic

quiz.q: A spacecraft finds that a rocky planet's average density is much higher than the density of the rocks on its surface. What is the best conclusion?
options: Its surface must be covered by young lava
It must have a thick atmosphere
Its interior must contain denser material, such as a metal core
It must be geologically dead
It must be made mostly of hydrogen and helium
quiz.why: If the whole planet is denser than its surface rock, something inside must be denser still, which points to a metal core. The comparison says nothing about lava, atmosphere or activity, and hydrogen and helium would make the average density low, not high.

quiz.q: Why are the terrestrial planets made mostly of rock and metal, even though the cloud they formed from was mostly hydrogen and helium?
options: Rock and metal made up most of the cloud
The inner planets did not collect the hydrogen and helium gas, so only the rare rock and metal built them
The Sun turned their hydrogen into rock
Comets later removed their hydrogen and helium oceans
quiz.why: About 98% of the cloud was hydrogen and helium, but the inner planets did not gather these gases, so they were built from the less than 1% that was rock and metal. Rock and metal were never the main part of the cloud, and the Sun does not convert a planet's gas into rock.

quiz.q: Which statement about Earth's lithosphere is correct?
options: It is the soft, partly molten layer that the plates ride on
It is the liquid layer between the mantle and the core
It is the crust alone, without any mantle rock
It is the cool, rigid outer layer made of the crust and the uppermost mantle
It is a thin layer of loose soil above the crust
quiz.why: The lithosphere is defined by strength: the cool, rigid rock of the crust plus the top of the mantle. The softer layer beneath is the asthenosphere, the liquid layer is the outer core, and leaving out the uppermost mantle makes it just the crust.

quiz.q: Two rocky worlds have the same composition, but one is much smaller. Compared with the larger one, the smaller world's lithosphere is most likely
options: thicker, because its interior has cooled more
thinner, because its weaker gravity cannot compress rock
the same thickness, because the rock is the same
missing, because small worlds have no crust
quiz.why: Small worlds lose heat faster, and cool rock is rigid, so the rigid lithosphere extends deeper; Mars, Mercury and the Moon have lithospheres reaching almost to their cores. Same rock does not mean same thickness, because temperature controls stiffness, and small worlds still have crusts.

quiz.q: A young planet is molten all the way through. What does gravity do to its iron and its lighter silicate rock?
options: The iron rises to form a metal shell because metals carry heat upward
The iron sinks toward the centre and the lighter rock rises toward the surface
Both stay evenly mixed, because gravity pulls on everything equally
The rock sinks to the centre and the iron forms the crust
quiz.why: This is differentiation: in a molten world denser material sinks and less dense material rises, like water and oil, giving a metal core under a rocky mantle and crust. Gravity pulls harder on each unit of the denser material compared with what it displaces, so the mixture does not stay even.

quiz.q: Which source still adds significant new heat to Earth's interior today?
options: Accretion of planetesimals
Differentiation of iron sinking to the core
Sunlight soaking down into the rock
Decay of radioactive elements such as uranium
Conduction through the lithosphere
quiz.why: Accretion and differentiation added their heat when Earth was young; only radioactive decay keeps releasing new heat. Sunlight warms only the top few metres, and conduction moves heat outward rather than making it.

quiz.q: Which list contains only processes that carry heat out of a planet rather than create it?
options: Convection, conduction and radiation
Accretion, differentiation and radioactive decay
Accretion, convection and radiation
Radioactive decay, conduction and radiation
quiz.why: Convection, conduction and radiation all move heat outward. Accretion, differentiation and radioactive decay are the sources that put heat in, so any list containing one of them mixes the two ideas.
quiz.source: Ch9.1 pt2 slides 2-4; Cosmic Perspective Figures 9.4 and 9.5

quiz.q: Hot rock rises from deep in Earth's mantle and reaches the bottom of the rigid lithosphere. How does the heat mostly continue upward from there?
options: By convection, because the lithosphere flows quickly
By radiation of infrared light through the solid rock
By conduction, passed from hotter rock to cooler rock by contact
By differentiation of dense material
quiz.why: Rigid rock cannot flow readily, so convection halts at the base of the lithosphere; heat gets through it mainly by conduction and then radiates from the surface. Light cannot shine through kilometres of rock, and differentiation is a heat source, not a way heat travels.
quiz.source: Ch9.1 pt2 slide 4; Cosmic Perspective Figure 9.5

quiz.q: Sphere A has a radius of 2 km and sphere B a radius of 6 km. How do their surface area-to-volume ratios compare, and which cools faster if both start equally hot?
options: B's ratio is 3 times A's, so B cools faster
A's ratio is 3 times B's, so A cools faster
A's ratio is 9 times B's, so A cools faster
The ratios are equal, so both cool at the same rate
quiz.why: For a sphere the ratio is 3/r: 3/2 = 1.5 per km for A and 3/6 = 0.5 per km for B, so A's is three times larger and A loses heat faster for the heat it holds. A factor of 9 would come from comparing areas alone (r²), and the ratios are not equal because they depend on r.
quiz.source: Ch9.1 pt2 slide 6; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 9.1

quiz.q: A sphere has a radius of 6 km and a volume of 288π km³. Using surface area ÷ volume = 3/r, what is its surface area?
options: 288π km²
48π km²
36π km²
96π km²
144π km²
quiz.why: The ratio is 3/6 = 0.5 per km, so surface area = 0.5 × 288π = 144π km². Check: 4π × 6² = 144π km². 288π repeats the volume, and the other values come from using the wrong radius or ratio.
quiz.source: Ch9.1 pt2 slide 6; Cosmic Perspective Mathematical Insight 9.1

quiz.q: Planet X has twice the radius of planet Y, and both are made of the same rock. Which prediction is best?
options: Y stays active longer, because heat leaks more slowly out of a small world
Both stay active equally long, because the same rock makes the same heat
X stays active longer only if it is closer to the Sun
X stays geologically active longer, because its surface area-to-volume ratio is half of Y's
quiz.why: Doubling r halves 3/r, so X has half as much surface per unit of stored heat and cools more slowly; it also starts with more heat. Heat escapes faster, not slower, from a small world, and internal activity depends on size, not on distance from the Sun.

quiz.q: Why is the Moon geologically dead today while Earth is still active?
options: The Moon is much older than Earth
The Moon has no gravity, so magma cannot rise
The small Moon lost its internal heat quickly, so its lithosphere thickened and convection stopped
Impacts destroyed the Moon's core
The Moon is too far from the Sun to melt rock
quiz.why: Size controls cooling: the small Moon cooled within about a billion years, its rigid layer thickened and mantle convection stopped. The Moon and Earth are about the same age, the Moon does have gravity, and internal melting does not come from sunlight.

quiz.q: If Earth's liquid outer core slowly froze solid, what would happen to its global magnetic field?
options: It would fade away, because no convecting, conducting fluid would be left to move charges
It would grow stronger, because solid iron is magnetic
It would not change, as long as Earth keeps rotating
It would become stronger at the equator than at the poles
quiz.why: The field is generated by electric charges moving with convecting molten metal. Freeze the core and that motion stops, so rotation alone cannot keep the field going. Hot iron in a planet's core does not act as a permanent magnet.

quiz.q: Venus is almost Earth's size and probably has a partly molten core, yet it has no global magnetic field. What is the most likely reason?
options: It is too close to the Sun
It rotates very slowly, about once every 243 days
Its core is made of rock rather than metal
Its thick atmosphere blocks magnetic fields
It is covered in craters
quiz.why: A field needs conducting fluid, convection and at least moderately rapid rotation; Venus's very slow spin (or too weak convection) is the missing piece. Its core is metal, distance from the Sun does not switch off a dynamo, and an atmosphere does not block a magnetic field.

quiz.q: Which terrestrial world meets all three requirements for a strong global magnetic field?
options: Mars
Mercury
the Moon
Earth
Venus
quiz.why: Only Earth has a convecting, conducting molten outer core and fairly fast rotation. The Moon and Mars have cooled too much for core convection, Venus spins too slowly, and Mercury's field is only weak.

quiz.q: How does Earth's magnetosphere help life on the surface?
options: It traps sunlight to keep the planet warm
It causes the seasons
It deflects the charged particles of the solar wind and helps keep the atmosphere from being stripped away
It pulls meteorites in so they burn up
quiz.why: The magnetosphere steers solar-wind particles around Earth (some reach the poles and make auroras), protecting the atmosphere and life. Warming comes from sunlight and the atmosphere, the seasons come from the axis tilt, and meteors burn up because of air friction, not magnetism.

quiz.q: An asteroid 3 km across hits a rocky moon. About how wide will the crater be?
options: About 3 km
About 3.5 km
About 300 km
About 3000 km
About 30 km
quiz.why: A crater usually ends up about 10 times wider than the object that made it, so 3 km × 10 ≈ 30 km. The same width or a little wider ignores the explosion, and 100 or 1000 times is far too large.

quiz.q: A crater on Mars has an unusually large central bump and is surrounded by flows that look like hardened mud. What does this most likely tell us?
options: The impact hit ground that held water or ice
The crater was made by a volcano, not an impact
It is the oldest crater on Mars
The impactor itself was made of mud
quiz.why: Mud-like flows suggest that underground water or ice melted on impact and the muddy debris spread and hardened. The shape is still an impact crater, age is judged from crater crowding not from flows, and impactors are rock, metal or ice, not mud.

quiz.q: Very runny lava erupts on a planet. Which landform is it most likely to build?
options: A steep-sided stratovolcano
Wide, flat volcanic plains
A deep ocean trench
A long rift valley
quiz.why: Runny (low-viscosity) lava flows far before hardening, so it spreads into flat plains like the lunar maria. Steep stratovolcanoes need thick lava, and trenches and rifts are tectonic features, not eruptions.

quiz.q: Mount Hood is a steep stratovolcano while Olympus Mons is a broad shield volcano. What best explains the difference in shape?
options: Mount Hood is much older
Olympus Mons erupted for a shorter time
Mount Hood's lava was thicker and flowed less easily
Mount Hood erupted more lava in total
Olympus Mons is on a smaller planet
quiz.why: Volcano steepness is set by lava viscosity: thick lava piles up steeply near the vent, while runnier lava spreads into a broad shield. Age, eruption length and total volume do not set the slope, and Olympus Mons is actually far taller than Mount Hood.

quiz.q: Where did nearly all the gas in the atmospheres of Venus, Earth and Mars originally come from?
options: Hydrogen and helium captured from the solar nebula
Gas blown onto them by the solar wind
Evaporation of ancient oceans of liquid nitrogen
Outgassing from the planets' interiors through volcanoes
quiz.why: Gas and water trapped inside the young planets were released by eruptions and volcanic vents. The terrestrial planets did not keep nebular hydrogen and helium, and the solar wind strips gas away rather than supplying it.

quiz.q: Which of these features was made by tectonics rather than erosion?
options: A canyon cut by a river
A rift valley where the crust is being pulled apart
A U-shaped valley carved by a glacier
A field of sand dunes
A river delta
quiz.why: A rift valley forms when internal stresses stretch and break the crust, which is tectonics. Rivers, glaciers and wind (canyons, glacial valleys, dunes) and river sediment (deltas) are all erosion.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of erosion building a feature up rather than wearing it down?
options: A river delta
A rift valley
A shield volcano
A crater's central peak
quiz.why: Erosion moves material as well as removing it: a delta is built from sediment that a river carried downstream. A rift valley is tectonic, a shield volcano is volcanic and a central peak is part of an impact crater.

quiz.q: On an orbital photo of a rocky world, region A is crowded with overlapping craters and region B is a smooth plain with only a few small craters. What is the best conclusion?
options: B's surface is younger: lava or another process erased its older craters
B's surface is older, because its craters had time to wear away
A was hit more because it faces the Sun
B is smooth because there were few impactors when the planet formed
Both surfaces must be the same age, because the planet formed all at once
quiz.why: Craters only build up with time and impacts fall everywhere at random, so a lightly cratered region must have been resurfaced more recently. Impacts do not favour the sunward side, the early impact rate was highest, and the planet's age is not the same thing as a surface's age.

quiz.q: Mercury is heavily cratered, while Venus has relatively few craters. Which statement is correct?
options: Venus formed much later than Mercury
Mercury's surface is younger than Venus's
Venus's surface is younger, although both planets formed at about the same time
Venus is never hit by asteroids or comets
quiz.why: Crater counts date surfaces, not planets. Venus is large enough to stay active, so volcanism and tectonics erased its old craters, while small Mercury kept its ancient ones. Both planets are about 4.5 billion years old, and Venus does get hit, as its craters show.

quiz.q: Why do larger terrestrial planets generally have more erosion?
options: They are always closer to the Sun
They have more craters to wear down
Their stronger gravity pulls rocks downhill faster
More outgassing and stronger gravity let them build and keep an atmosphere, which brings wind and rain
quiz.why: Erosion needs weather, and weather needs an atmosphere. Big worlds outgas more and their gravity holds the gas. Size does not set distance from the Sun, crater numbers do not cause erosion, and downhill pull alone does not make wind and rain.

quiz.q: Two planets have the same size and composition, but one spins once a day and the other once every 200 days. Which difference is expected?
options: The slow spinner has more erosion, because its days are longer
The fast spinner has more wind, more erosion and a better chance of a strong magnetic field
The slow spinner has the stronger magnetic field
Both have the same weather, because rotation does not affect wind
quiz.why: Rotation drives winds and storms, so the fast spinner has more weather and erosion, and moderately rapid rotation is needed for a strong global field. Slow rotation means less weather and a weaker field even with a molten core.

quiz.q: An Earth-sized planet orbits far from its star, where it is very cold. Why would it have little erosion even with an atmosphere?
options: It is too cold for rain or liquid oceans, so water is locked up as ice and snow
It cannot have any wind
Its gravity is too weak to hold gas
It would have too much liquid water
quiz.why: Far from the Sun, water and other gases freeze out, so there is no rain and no flowing water, the most effective eroder. An Earth-sized planet has enough gravity to keep an atmosphere and can still have some wind, but liquid water is what is missing.

quiz.q: Seafloor crust is rarely older than about 200 million years, but some continental rock is nearly 4 billion years old. Why?
options: Ocean water dissolves old seafloor rock
The oceans formed only 200 million years ago
Dense seafloor crust is carried back into the mantle at subduction zones, while lighter continental crust stays on top
Hot ocean water melts the seafloor from above
quiz.why: The seafloor is part of a conveyor belt: made at mid-ocean ridges and destroyed by subduction, so none of it survives very long. Continental crust is too light to sink. Ocean water erodes the deep sea floor very little, and Earth has had oceans for billions of years.

quiz.q: Which feature marks a place where a seafloor plate is sinking beneath another plate?
options: A deep ocean trench
A mid-ocean ridge
A continental rift valley
A sideways-slipping fault such as the San Andreas
A hot-spot island chain
quiz.why: Subduction drags the sea floor down into a trench. Ridges and rifts are where plates pull apart, transform faults are where plates move sideways, and hot-spot islands form inside a plate over a mantle plume.

quiz.q: The Himalayas are still getting taller today. Why?
options: A hot spot under Tibet keeps erupting new lava
Erosion piles sediment higher every year
The plates there are pulling apart
The Indian plate keeps pushing into the Eurasian plate, and neither continental plate can sink
quiz.why: At a continent-continent convergent boundary the light crust cannot subduct, so the collision crumples it upward, and the collision is still going on. A hot spot builds volcanoes, erosion lowers mountains, and pulling apart makes rifts, not mountains.

quiz.q: If the East African Rift keeps widening for many millions of years, what is expected to happen?
options: It turns into a mountain range like the Himalayas
The rift floods and becomes a new sea with seafloor spreading, as the Red Sea did
It becomes a deep subduction trench
It is filled in and erased by sand dunes
quiz.why: A continental rift is a divergent boundary: as Africa splits, rising mantle rock erupts on the valley floor and the sea floods in, just as the Red Sea opened between Africa and Arabia. Mountains and trenches belong to convergent boundaries, and erosion cannot stop the plates moving apart.

quiz.q: A plate moves 3 cm per year. About how far does it travel in 100 million years?
options: About 3 km
About 30 km
About 3000 km
About 300,000 km
About 30 m
quiz.why: 3 cm × 100,000,000 = 300,000,000 cm = 3,000,000 m = 3000 km. Slow motion becomes huge distances over geological time, which is how the Atlantic opened. The other answers slip by factors of 1000 or more.

quiz.q: In the Hawaiian chain the Big Island has fresh lava, Kauai is deeply eroded and Midway is worn almost to sea level. What does this pattern show?
options: The Pacific plate is moving over a hot spot that stays in place, so islands farther northwest are older
All the islands formed at the same time, but the northwest gets more rain
The islands formed at a subduction trench and are sinking into it
Each island formed at its own boundary where plates pull apart
quiz.why: A mantle plume stays put while the Pacific plate moves northwest over it, so the youngest island sits over the plume and older ones have been carried away and eroded for millions of years. Hawaii is in the middle of a plate, not at a trench or a divergent boundary, and the islands clearly differ in age.

quiz.q: Which world's surface is shaped mainly by ongoing plate tectonics?
options: Earth only
Earth and Venus
Earth and Mars
All five terrestrial worlds
quiz.why: Tectonics of some kind has happened on every terrestrial world, but plate tectonics, with a lithosphere broken into moving plates, is known only on Earth. Venus is nearly Earth's size yet shows no plate tectonics.

quiz.q: The lithosphere of a planet is the layer that consists of
options: material between the crust and the mantle.
the rigid rocky material of the crust and uppermost portion of the mantle.
material above the crust.
the lava that comes out of volcanoes.
the softer rocky material of the mantle.
quiz.why: Think of the lithosphere as a planet's stiff outer shell: the crust together with the cold top layer of the mantle beneath it. What sets the boundary is how stiff the rock is, not what chemicals it contains. The softer rock below it is the asthenosphere, the crust is only part of the lithosphere, and lava is just molten rock that erupts.

quiz.q: How do scientists learn about the internal composition of our planet?
options: They collect seismic data to infer the densities and thicknesses of different regions in the Earth's interior.
They use x-ray and gamma ray imaging, which can penetrate the Earth's surface.
They drill into the earth with state-of-the-art equipment to collect samples from deep within the Earth's interior.
They drop special, heat-resistant probes into volcanoes to explore and obtain data from underneath the Earth's crust.
quiz.why: We cannot drill deep or see inside, so scientists use seismic waves from earthquakes. Their speeds and paths depend on density and on whether the material is solid or liquid, which reveals the layers inside Earth. X-rays and gamma rays do not penetrate far, drills reach less than 1% of the way to the centre, and probes cannot be dropped into volcanoes that deep.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes differentiation in planetary geology?
options: One planet's surface evolves differently from another planet's surface.
Different types of minerals form a conglomerate rock.
Gravity separates molten materials according to density.
One part of a planet's surface evolves differently from another part of the same planet's surface.
Dense materials condense at higher temperatures than less dense materials.
quiz.why: Differentiation happens when a planet is molten enough that gravity separates material by density: dense metals sink to the core and lighter rock rises to form the mantle and crust, like oil and water separating. The other options mix this up with how surfaces evolve, how rocks form or how materials condense.

quiz.q: Which internal energy source is the most important in continuing to heat the terrestrial planets today?
options: accretion
differentiation
tidal heating
radioactivity
quiz.why: Heat from accretion and differentiation was mostly deposited when the planets were young, while radioactive decay of uranium, potassium and thorium is still releasing heat, so it is the main source now. Tidal heating matters for moons such as Io, but not for the terrestrial planets.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes convection?
options: Warm material expands and rises while cool material contracts and falls.
Bubbles of gas move upward through a liquid of the same temperature.
A liquid separates according to density, such as oil and water separating in a jar.
Rocks sink in water.
Warm material gets even warmer and cool material gets even cooler.
quiz.why: Convection is the process in which warm material expands and rises while cooler material contracts and falls, carrying heat upward, as in a pot of soup or in Earth's mantle. Gas bubbles rising, a liquid separating by density and rocks sinking in water are other ideas, and in convection warm material does not simply warm up more.

quiz.q: What are the three main sources of internal heat for terrestrial planets?
options: convection, differentiation, and eruption
conduction, differentiation, and accretion
accretion, differentiation, and eruption
conduction, convection, and eruption
accretion, differentiation, and radioactivity
quiz.why: Terrestrial planets get internal heat from accretion (impacts of planetesimals), differentiation (dense material sinking) and radioactive decay. Convection, conduction and eruption are ways heat moves or escapes, not sources of heat.

quiz.q: What conditions are thought to be necessary for a terrestrial planet to have a strong magnetic field?
options: fast rotation only
both a metal core and a rocky mantle
a molten metallic core only
a rocky mantle only
both a molten metallic core and reasonably fast rotation
quiz.why: A strong magnetic field needs an electrically conducting fluid such as molten metal, convection in it, and reasonably fast rotation. Earth has a molten outer core and rotates in a day, so it has a strong field. A molten core alone is not enough (Venus rotates very slowly), fast rotation alone is not enough, and a metal core with a rocky mantle can be solid, as with the Moon and Mars.

quiz.q: What is the main process by which heat flows upward through the lithosphere?
options: conduction
differentiation
convection
radiation
accretion
quiz.why: Inside the rigid lithosphere the rock cannot flow, so mantle convection stops at its base and heat moves upward mainly by conduction, atom to atom through contact, and is then radiated into space. Differentiation and accretion are heat sources, convection occurs below the lithosphere, and radiation is how the heat leaves from the surface into space.

quiz.q: If a spherical body has a surface area of 36π km², what is its volume? (Recall that the surface area-to-volume ratio of a sphere is 3/r.)
options: 216 km³
36π km³
10π km³
3 km³
quiz.why: A sphere's surface area is 4πr². If 4πr² = 36π, then r² = 9 and r = 3 km. The surface area to volume ratio is 3/r = 1 per km, so volume = surface area ÷ ratio = 36π km² ÷ (1 per km) = 36π km³. Check: (4/3)π(3)³ = 36π km³. The 216 km³ choice cubes the diameter (6³) instead of using (4/3)πr³, and 3 km³ is just the number 3/r, not a volume.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an effect of a planet having a larger size?
options: The planet undergoes internal geological activity for longer.
The planet retains an atmosphere for longer and experiences more erosion.
The planet has a warmer surface temperature.
The planet loses heat less quickly.
quiz.why: A larger planet keeps its interior heat longer, so it stays geologically active longer, and its stronger gravity holds an atmosphere longer, leading to more erosion. Surface temperature is not an effect of size, because it depends mainly on distance from the Sun and on the atmosphere. Earth and Venus are almost the same size but have very different surface temperatures.

quiz.q: Which terrestrial world has the strongest magnetic field?
options: the Moon
Venus
Mars
Mercury
Earth
quiz.why: Earth has a molten, convecting metal outer core and rotates fairly quickly, so it has a strong global magnetic field. The Moon and Mars have cooled too much to have such a core, Venus rotates too slowly, and Mercury has only a weak field.

quiz.q: Approximately how large (across) is an impact crater compared to the size of the impactor?
options: 10 times larger
100 times larger
the same size
1000 times larger
10—20 percent larger
quiz.why: Because the impactor explodes on contact and blasts out material all around, the crater ends up roughly ten times wider than the object that hit. For example, a 1 km asteroid makes a crater about 10 km across. The other sizes are too large or too small.

quiz.q: Which factor below determines the steepness of a volcano?
options: the duration of the eruption
the age of the volcano
the temperature of the lava
the volume of lava
how easily the lava flows
quiz.why: Thick, sticky lava cannot flow far, so it piles up into steep stratovolcanoes, while runny lava spreads out into gently sloping shield volcanoes or flat lava plains. Steepness is set by how easily the lava flows (its viscosity), not by how long the volcano erupted, its age or the total volume of lava.

quiz.q: A planet is most likely to have volcanic and tectonic activity if it has
options: low internal temperature.
high internal temperature.
high surface gravity.
low surface gravity.
a dense atmosphere.
quiz.why: Volcanism and tectonics are driven by internal heat, which melts rock and drives mantle convection. So a planet with a high internal temperature is most likely to be active. A low internal temperature leads to a geologically dead planet, and surface gravity or a thick atmosphere does not drive volcanism.

quiz.q: What can we conclude when we see a region of a planet that is not as heavily cratered as other regions?
options: There is little volcanic activity to create craters.
The surface in the region is younger than the surface in more heavily cratered regions.
The planet is rotating very slowly and only one side was hit by impactors.
The surface in the region is older than the surface in more heavily cratered regions.
The planet formed after the age of bombardment and missed out on getting hit by leftover planetesimals.
quiz.why: Craters build up over time, so a region with fewer craters must have been resurfaced more recently, for example by lava or erosion, which erased older craters. That makes it younger than a heavily cratered region. Volcanic activity erases craters rather than makes them, and planets do not get impacts on only one side.

quiz.q: Which of the following natural geological features is NOT a result of erosion?
options: Sand dunes
Canyons
Fjords
Rift valleys
River deltas
quiz.why: Rift valleys form when tectonic forces pull the crust apart, not by erosion. Canyons are cut by rivers, fjords are valleys carved by glaciers, sand dunes are shaped by wind and river deltas are built from sediment carried by water, so all of these come from erosion.

quiz.q: What is the overall geological process occurring at the Great Rift Valley in Africa?
options: Continental crust is pushing together at a convergent plate boundary.
Ocean crust is subducting under continental crust.
Continental crust is being pulled apart at a divergent plate boundary.
Two tectonic plates are sliding past each other, resulting in earthquakes.
quiz.why: The Great Rift Valley in East Africa is where continental crust is being pulled apart at a divergent boundary, thinning the crust so a rift valley forms, and eventually the continent could split. Convergent boundaries push together, subduction is an ocean plate going under another plate, and sliding past is a transform fault like the San Andreas.

quiz.q: What process has played the greatest role in determining the arrangement of the continents on Earth?
options: impact cratering
acid rain
erosion
volcanism
plate tectonics
quiz.why: The slow movement of tectonic plates over millions of years has carried the continents into their present arrangement. Impacts, acid rain, erosion and volcanism shape surfaces but do not move continents.

quiz.q: On average, approximately how fast do plates move with plate tectonics on Earth?
options: They do not move at all, except during earthquakes.
a few centimeters per year
a few millimeters per century
a few centimeters per century
a few kilometers per hour
quiz.why: Tectonic plates move a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow. That is slow, but over millions of years it moves continents thousands of kilometers. Plates are not stationary except in earthquakes, and a few millimeters per century or a few centimeters per century are far too slow, while a few kilometers per hour is much too fast.

quiz.q: Deep trenches in the ocean mark places where
options: one plate moves under another, returning older crust to the mantle.
plates pull apart, leaving great rifts in the crust.
plates push together, creating ocean mountain chains.
hot mantle material rises upward and spreads sideways, pushing the plates apart.
plates slip sideways relative to one another.
quiz.why: Deep ocean trenches mark subduction zones, where the denser plate of seafloor crust moves under another plate and is returned to the mantle. Plates pulling apart make rifts and mid-ocean ridges, plates pushing together can make mountains, and plates sliding sideways make faults.

quiz.q: The islands of Hawaii were created by
options: a plate that has run up against an existing continental plate.
a fault.
plumes of hot mantle rising in a hot spot within a plate.
plates that have slipped sideways relative to each other, creating a fault.
thin continental crust separating and creating a rift valley.
quiz.why: The Hawaiian Islands formed over a hot spot, a plume of hot mantle rising inside the Pacific plate. As the plate moves over the hot spot, new volcanoes build islands in a chain. Hawaii is not on a plate boundary, so a fault, a collision or a rift valley is not the cause.

quiz.q: Which of the following properties is MOST important in determining the boundary between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere of the Earth?
options: rock strength and temperature
chemical composition
density
physical state (liquid, solid)
geological age
quiz.why: The lithosphere is cool, rigid rock; the asthenosphere below is warmer, softer rock that can flow slowly. Both are solid and similar in makeup, so the boundary is set by temperature and strength.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements about the heating of Earth's interior is NOT true?
options: Radioactivity is the dominant source of internal heating today.
Impacts during accretion and the heavy bombardment released enormous quantities of heat in the past, but this heat has since completely dissipated.
Differentiation was once a major heat source, but no longer contributes much to Earth's internal heat budget.
Convection does not produce any heat within Earth's interior.
Eventually, all radioactive elements on Earth will decay, differentiation will cease, and all internal heat sources will be exhausted, rendering Earth geologically dead.
quiz.why: Heat from accretion has not completely escaped: a large planet like Earth keeps part of its early heat for billions of years, which is one reason it is still active. Radioactive decay is the main heat source today, and convection only moves heat, it does not make it.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements regarding differentiation and convection in geology is TRUE?
options: Differentiation only involves material sinking, but convection involves material both rising and sinking.
Differentiation occurs throughout the interior of a planet, but convection takes place only in the core.
Differentiation involves rocks and metals, but convection involves magma (liquid rock).
Differentiation concluded long ago, but convection continues to this day.
Differentiation involves the large-scale movement of material, but convection is a microscopic heat transport process.
quiz.why: Differentiation (dense metal sinking to the core, lighter rock rising) happened early in Earth's history. Mantle convection, slow flow of hot solid rock, still goes on today. Light material also rises during differentiation, and convection is large scale and mostly in solid rock.

quiz.q: Which of the following BEST describes why Mercury does NOT have a strong magnetic field?
options: Mercury has a large iron core relative to its size.
Mercury has a very long day.
Mercury is too close to the Sun, leading to the erosion of its magnetic field by the solar wind.
Mercury has very little atmosphere.
Mercury's temperature gradient interferes with the generation of a strong magnetic field.
quiz.why: A strong magnetic field needs a convecting, electrically conducting core and fairly rapid rotation. Mercury rotates very slowly (its day lasts months), so its field is weak despite its large iron core.

quiz.q: Jupiter's moon Callisto has many more craters on its surface than either Io or Europa. What can we conclude from this?
options: Callisto has been struck by many more impactors than Io or Europa.
Callisto's surface is much younger, likely because geological processes on Io and Europa have had time to erode those moons' craters.
Callisto's surface is much older, likely because geological processes on Io and Europa continuously repave their surfaces.
Callisto's surface is much older, likely because the moon itself is older than Io or Europa.
The moon is farther out in its orbit than the others, which explains why it gets struck more often.
quiz.why: More craters means an older surface. All three moons are the same age, but volcanism on Io and ice activity on Europa keep erasing craters, while geologically dead Callisto keeps every one.

quiz.q: Suppose you discover chasms on a rocky exoplanet that stretch for hundreds of kilometers. The planet has no substantial atmosphere but is twice as massive as Earth. Which is a reasonable hypothesis for the origin of the chasms?
options: They are a result of impacts to the surface from asteroids coming in at a glancing blow.
They are a result of erosion, as these planetary conditions permit a water cycle.
They are a result of volcanism, as lava flows can carve deep channels in softer rock.
They are a result of tectonic activity, as internal heat is likely high enough for large-scale surface disruption.
They are a result of atmospheric processes such as storms that can crack the landscape.
quiz.why: A planet twice Earth's mass keeps plenty of internal heat, so tectonic stretching and cracking of its crust is likely. With no atmosphere there is no water cycle or storms, so erosion and weather are ruled out.

quiz.q: On what kind of world would we expect to see evidence of erosion?
options: On a large planet far enough from its host star to freeze water, with a high rotation rate (short day) and lots of atmosphere.
On a small planet close enough to its host star to vaporize water, with a slow rotation rate (long day) and little atmosphere.
On a large planet at a suitable distance from its host star to allow multiple phases of water to coexist, with a high rotation rate (short day) and lots of atmosphere.
On a small planet far enough from its host star to freeze water, with a high rotation rate (short day) and little atmosphere.
On a large planet at a suitable distance from its host star to allow multiple phases of water to coexist, with a slow rotation rate (long day) and lots of atmosphere.
quiz.why: Erosion needs weather: a thick atmosphere (large size helps hold one), water that can rain, flow and freeze, and fast rotation, which drives strong winds and storms.

quiz.q: Which of the following is by itself NOT evidence for plate tectonics on Earth?
options: Seismic data shows that most strong earthquakes happen along long fault lines that connect together, dividing Earth's surface.
Some continental boundaries, and especially their continental shelves, fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle.
Numerous mountains and active volcanoes are found across the Earth's surface.
Similar rocks and fossils are found in different continents.
Satellites detect incremental movement of different large landmasses.
quiz.why: Mountains and volcanoes alone do not prove moving plates: Mars and Venus have them without plate tectonics. Linked earthquake belts, fitting coastlines, matching fossils and measured drift all point to plates.

quiz.q: Mid-ocean ridges are places where
options: hot mantle material rises upward and spreads sideways, pushing the plates apart.
one plate sinks beneath another, returning older crust to the mantle.
plates slip sideways relative to one another.
hot mantle material rises upward, creating volcanic islands.
plates push together, creating ocean mountain chains.
quiz.why: At mid-ocean ridges hot mantle rock wells up and spreads outward, making new sea floor and pushing plates apart. Sinking beneath is subduction; sideways slipping is a transform fault; rising plumes making islands are hot spots.

order.title: Earth's layers by depth
order.prompt: Put Earth's layers in order from the deepest at the bottom to the surface at the top.
order.why: The solid inner core sits at the centre (down to 6378 km), wrapped in the liquid outer core (from about 5100 km up to 2900 km). Above it is the mantle; its upper part includes the soft asthenosphere, and above that is the rigid uppermost mantle that, together with the crust, forms the lithosphere.

order.title: How long each world stays active
order.prompt: Order the terrestrial worlds by how much geological activity they keep, from the least at the bottom to the most at the top.
order.why: Size decides how long a world keeps its internal heat. The tiny Moon and small Mercury are geologically dead, Mars is in between and has much less activity than in the past, Venus is almost Earth's size and is probably still active, and Earth, the largest, is the most active.

order.title: Heat on its way out
order.prompt: Follow heat from where it is made to where it leaves the planet. Put the first step at the bottom and the last at the top.
order.why: Radioactive decay heats the deep rock; that hot rock rises in mantle convection cells; convection stops at the base of the rigid lithosphere; the heat crosses the lithosphere by conduction; finally it leaves the surface as infrared radiation.

layers.name: Hot mantle rock rises in a convection cell
Rising rock reaches the base of the lithosphere
Heat crosses the lithosphere by conduction
Heat leaves the surface as infrared light

order.title: Life of a piece of seafloor
order.prompt: Put the life of a piece of seafloor crust in order, with the first event at the bottom and the last at the top.
order.why: Mantle rock rises at a mid-ocean ridge and erupts as new basalt crust, then spreads away from the ridge across the ocean over tens of millions of years. At a trench it is pushed under a continent and sinks into the mantle, where part of it melts and feeds volcanoes on the continent's edge.

layers.name: Mantle rock rises under a mid-ocean ridge
It erupts as new seafloor crust
It spreads across the ocean floor
Partly melted, it feeds coastal volcanoes

sort.title: Which process made it?
sort.prompt: Sort each landform by the geological process that made it.

items.text: A ring of debris around a fresh crater
Lava plains of the lunar maria

sort.why: Craters and their peaks come from impacts; lava plains, shields, stratovolcanoes and hot-spot islands from volcanism; mountains, rifts, tectonic canyons and faults from stresses in the crust; and canyons cut by rivers, glacial valleys, fjords, dunes and deltas from erosion by water, ice and wind.

sort.title: Heat source or heat mover?
sort.prompt: Sort each item by whether it adds heat to a planet's interior or moves heat outward.

items.text: Planetesimals crashing into a young planet

sort.why: Accretion (impacts), differentiation (sinking metal) and radioactive decay are the three heat sources. Convection, conduction and radiation, helped by eruptions, carry the heat out to space.

sort.title: Larger or smaller world?
sort.prompt: Sort each feature by whether it fits a larger or a smaller terrestrial world, if everything else is the same.
sort.why: A larger world has a smaller surface area-to-volume ratio, so it cools slowly, keeps a thin lithosphere, stays volcanically and tectonically active, outgasses and holds an atmosphere, and erases its old craters. A small world cools fast, thickens its lithosphere, goes dead and keeps its craters.

sort.title: Which kind of plate boundary?
sort.prompt: Sort each place or feature by the kind of plate boundary it belongs to.

items.text: Plates sliding sideways past each other

sort.why: Plates push together at convergent boundaries (trenches, subduction, the Andes, the Himalayas), pull apart at divergent boundaries (ridges, rifts, the Red Sea, Iceland) and move sideways past each other at transform boundaries such as the San Andreas Fault.
